title: The Sun can hurl over a billion tonnes of its atmosphere into space at once

cover.alt: Close-up of the Sun’s glowing orange edge in ultraviolet light, with a long dark strand of gas curving above the surface.
cover.credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/SDO · Public domain

body: A coronal mass ejection, or CME, is a vast cloud of magnetised plasma blasted out of the Sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. The average one carries about **1.6 billion tonnes** of material, and they fly off at anything from 20 to 3,200 km/s. Most are linked to erupting prominences: long strands of cooler, denser gas that magnetic fields hold up above the Sun until they suddenly break loose. A CME heading our way typically reaches Earth one to five days later, where it can rattle Earth’s magnetic field and set off geomagnetic storms.

slides.alt: Close-up of the Sun’s edge in orange ultraviolet light: a dark, curving strand of gas hangs above the surface, then snaps loose and streams off into space, leaving bright glowing loops behind.
slides.caption: 31 August 2012: a long filament of gas that had been hovering in the Sun’s atmosphere breaks loose and flies off at over 1,400 km/s. NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory, at half speed.
slides.credit: NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center/SDO · Public domain · excerpt, slowed to half speed
slides.music: “Stay the Course” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.question: Near the peak of its 11-year cycle, about how many CMEs does the Sun launch per day?
slides.explanation: About 3.5 a day near solar maximum, but only about 0.2 a day, or one every five days, near solar minimum.

slides.note: Speeds measured across the sky; the 2012 eruption in the clip topped 1,400 km/s

slides.question: The first CME ever seen was spotted on 14 December 1971. What saw it?
slides.explanation: The coronagraph on Orbiting Solar Observatory 7 blocked the Sun’s bright disc, so the faint cloud racing away from it could be seen.
